blocks.text:
### How to use this guide

- **Who this is for.** A Java full stack developer who must explain, and diagnose, what the operating system does beneath a running service: process and thread management, memory, files, I/O, containers and synchronisation.
- **Every chapter follows the same steps:** (1) the concept and the problem it solves, (2) the mechanism, shown with diagrams, (3) a worked trace or calculation, (4) a hands-on experiment with real commands, C or Java code, (5) **real-world incidents**, each presented as symptoms, diagnosis, root cause, fix and prevention, and (6) the questions interviewers ask, with answers.
- **How to study.** Read each diagram before the prose and narrate it aloud. Reproduce every experiment on a Linux machine or virtual machine (never on a production host). Treat each incident as an exercise: cover the diagnosis, decide which command to run first, then compare with the text.
- **Running the code.** Save a Java listing as `Main.java` and run `java Main.java`; compile C with `gcc -O0 -o demo` `demo.c`. Terminal sessions begin with `$`. Output shown was produced on the build machine unless labelled typical.
- **Scope.** The focus is Linux, the platform on which most Java services run, together with the JVM and container behaviour that interacts with it. Windows and macOS are mentioned only where the difference matters.

The introductory material describes dependency injection as a service: classes declare what they need and the container supplies it. This chapter examines the machinery behind that service. Every production defect that mentions a "circular reference", a "bean not found", an "ambiguous dependency" or "a configuration that is ignored" is a defect in how bean definitions are registered, ordered, instantiated or wrapped. A developer who can name the classes involved and the sequence of calls can read a stack trace as a trace of a known algorithm instead of an opaque failure.

The container performs three distinct jobs, and keeping them apart clarifies most behaviour. First, it **collects** **metadata**: it reads annotations, Java configuration and imports, and converts them into `BeanDefinition` objects. Second, it **post-processes metadata**: components that implement `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` may rewrite the definitions before any application object exists. Third, it **creates and decorates objects**: the container instantiates beans, injects dependencies, runs callbacks, and allows `BeanPostProcessor` implementations to replace the raw object with a wrapper (a proxy). Each job has its own extension point, and a defect almost always belongs to exactly one of them.

### Concept and mechanism

#### BeanDefinition, BeanFactory and ApplicationContext

A `BeanDefinition` is a recipe: the bean class or factory method, scope, lazy flag, constructor arguments, property values, init and destroy method names, dependency names (`@DependsOn`), and autowire candidate flags. The concrete implementations are `GenericBeanDefinition`, `RootBeanDefinition` (the merged, runtime view used for creation), `AnnotatedGenericBeanDefinition` and `ScannedGenericBeanDefinition` (produced by component scanning, carrying annotation metadata read from bytecode without loading the class).

`BeanFactory` is the minimal contract (`getBean`, `containsBean`, `isSingleton`, `getType`). The implementation that does the work is `DefaultListableBeanFactory`, which is also a `BeanDefinitionRegistry`. `ApplicationContext` extends the factory contract with message resolution (`MessageSource`), event publication (`ApplicationEventPublisher`), resource loading (`ResourcePatternResolver`), and an `Environment`. Concrete contexts do not inherit from the factory; they delegate to an internal `DefaultListableBeanFactory`. In a servlet web application Spring Boot creates an `AnnotationConfigServletWebServerApplicationContext`.

blocks.text:
A practical consequence: `getBean()` on a context is a method of the delegated factory, and the first call for a singleton name creates the object, while later calls return the cached instance. Beans created eagerly at start-up are produced by `preInstantiateSingletons()`, which iterates over all definitions that are non-lazy singletons.

#### The refresh() algorithm

`SpringApplication.run()` creates the context and calls `AbstractApplicationContext.refresh()`. This method is a template with a fixed order of steps, and the order explains which extension point can see which objects.

rows: Initialises property sources, validates required properties, creates the early event set.
Returns the DefaultListableBeanFactory (for a GenericApplicationContext it already exists).
Registers environment beans, Aware processors (ApplicationContextAwareProcessor), resolvable dependencies such as BeanFactory and ApplicationContext.
Subclass hook; web contexts register request and session scopes here.
Runs BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor, then BeanFactoryPostProcessor. ConfigurationClassPostProcessor parses @Configuration, @ComponentScan, @Import and @Bean here.
Instantiates all BeanPostProcessor beans and sorts them (PriorityOrdered, Ordered, rest).
Subclass hook; ServletWebServerApplicationContext creates the embedded Tomcat here (not yet started accepting traffic).
Registers ApplicationListener beans with the multicaster.
Freezes configuration and calls preInstantiateSingletons(): all non-lazy singletons are created.
Starts Lifecycle beans (SmartLifecycle, including the web server) and publishes ContextRefreshedEvent.

Step 5 is the origin of most "why was my annotation ignored" questions. `ConfigurationClassPostProcessor` is a `BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor`: it reads every configuration candidate, recursively processes `@Import`, `@ImportResource` and `@ComponentScan`, evaluates `@Conditional` annotations, and registers the resulting `BeanDefinition` objects through `ConfigurationClassBeanDefinitionReader`. Auto-configuration enters at this point through `AutoConfigurationImportSelector`, a `DeferredImportSelector` that is processed after all user configuration so that `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` can observe user-defined beans.

#### BeanFactoryPostProcessor and BeanPostProcessor

The two interfaces have similar names and fundamentally different targets.

blocks.text:
When a `@Bean` method for a post-processor is non-static, the container must instantiate the enclosing configuration class to call it, and that class is then created too early to be processed by later post-processors. The container logs `Bean` `'x' of type [...] is not eligible for getting processed by all BeanPostProcessors` at INFO level. The corrective action is `static`.

#### The complete bean lifecycle

Instance creation is implemented in `AbstractAutowireCapableBeanFactory.doCreateBean()`. The phases, in the order executed for a singleton declared with a constructor and field injection, are:

1. `InstantiationAwareBeanPostProcessor.postProcessBeforeInstantiation` may return a replacement object and short-circuit everything below.
2. Instance creation: `createBeanInstance` selects a constructor (`AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor.determineCandidateConstructors`), a factory method, or an instance supplier.
3. `MergedBeanDefinitionPostProcessor.postProcessMergedBeanDefinition` collects injection metadata and lifecycle method metadata.
4. An early-reference factory is registered when the bean is a singleton in creation and circular references are allowed (see the section on circular dependencies).
5. `populateBean`: `postProcessAfterInstantiation`, then `postProcessProperties`, where `@Autowired` and `@Value` fields and setters are injected.
6. `initializeBean`: Aware callbacks (`BeanNameAware`, `BeanClassLoaderAware`, `BeanFactoryAware`), then `postProcessBeforeInitialization` of every `BeanPostProcessor` (this includes `ApplicationContextAware` and `EnvironmentAware`, applied by `ApplicationContextAwareProcessor`, and `@PostConstruct`, applied by `CommonAnnotationBeanPostProcessor`), then `InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet`, then the custom init method (`@Bean(initMethod = ...)`), then `postProcessAfterInitialization` of every `BeanPostProcessor`. AOP proxies are created in this last step, which is why the bean visible to other beans can be a different object from the one the constructor produced.
7. After all singletons exist: `SmartInitializingSingleton.afterSingletonsInstantiated`.
8. On `close()`: `@PreDestroy`, `DisposableBean.destroy`, the custom destroy method. For `@Bean` methods the destroy method is inferred when a public no-argument `close` or `shutdown` method exists.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: Prototype-scoped beans are created, injected and then abandoned: the container holds no reference and never invokes destruction callbacks for them. Resources held by a prototype bean must be released by the code that requested the bean.

#### Scopes and scoped proxies

The default scope is `singleton`: one instance per container (not per class loader or JVM). `prototype` creates a new instance for each injection point or `getBean` call. Web-aware scopes are `request`, `session`, `application` and `websocket`. Custom scopes implement `org.springframework.beans.factory.config.Scope`.

A singleton that needs a shorter-lived bean has a structural problem: the singleton is constructed once, so a plain injection captures exactly one instance. Two correct solutions exist. The first is a **scoped proxy**: the container injects a singleton proxy that, on every method call, resolves the real target from the current scope (`@RequestScope` is shorthand for `@Scope(value = "request", proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS)`). The second is **on-demand lookup** with `ObjectProvider<T>`, which calls `getObject()` when needed.

blocks.text:
#### Circular dependencies and the three-level cache

A cycle exists when bean A needs B and B needs A. With **constructor injection** no solution exists in principle: neither object can be constructed before the other. Spring throws `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException`. With **field or setter** **injection** the objects can be created first and wired afterwards, and `DefaultSingletonBeanRegistry` supports this using three maps:

- `singletonObjects` (level 1): completely initialised singletons.
- `earlySingletonObjects` (level 2): early references that were already handed out to another bean.
- `singletonFactories` (level 3): `ObjectFactory` callbacks that produce an early reference on demand.

When A is instantiated, a factory for A's raw instance is placed in level 3 before A's dependencies are populated. When B requires A, the lookup finds A in creation, calls the level-3 factory, moves the result to level 2, and injects it. The factory indirection exists so that `getEarlyBeanReference` can apply `SmartInstantiationAwareBeanPostProcessor` logic, for example to create the AOP proxy early so that B receives the same proxy that other beans will later receive.

Since Spring Boot 2.6 circular references are prohibited by default (`spring.main.allow-circular-references=false`), because a cycle indicates a design problem and because early references interact poorly with post-processors that do not support early exposure. A bean wrapped by `@Async` after an early reference was handed out produces the failure "has been injected into other beans in its raw version as part of a circular reference, but has eventually been wrapped".

blocks.text:
#### @Configuration proxying, lite mode and conditional registration

A class annotated `@Configuration` is, by default, subclassed at start-up with CGLIB (`ConfigurationClassEnhancer`). Calls to one `@Bean` method from another are intercepted by `BeanMethodInterceptor`, which returns the container's singleton instead of executing the method body again. This is **full mode** (`proxyBeanMethods = true`). In **lite mode** (`@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)`, or `@Bean` methods declared in a `@Component`) the class is not subclassed and inter-bean method calls are ordinary Java calls that create a fresh object each time. Spring Boot's own auto-configuration uses `proxyBeanMethods = false` for faster start-up; the safe style is to pass dependencies as method parameters, which works in both modes.

`@Conditional` registers or skips a definition by evaluating a `Condition.matches(ConditionContext,` `AnnotatedTypeMetadata)` call during configuration parsing. `@Profile`, `@ConditionalOnProperty` and `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` are all implementations of this single mechanism (the Boot conditions are examined in the chapter on auto-configuration).

#### Events, listeners and ordering

The context is an `ApplicationEventPublisher`. Any object can be published (since Spring 4.2); listeners are `ApplicationListener<E>` beans or methods annotated `@EventListener`. The default `SimpleApplicationEventMulticaster` invokes listeners **synchronously on the publishing thread**, in the order given by `@Order`. A listener that throws propagates the exception to the publisher unless an error handler is configured. Asynchronous delivery requires `@Async` on the listener method (which makes it a proxy case, see the next chapter) or an executor on the multicaster. Transaction-bound delivery with `@TransactionalEventListener` is covered in the chapter on transactions.

Spring Boot publishes a sequence of its own events during start-up: `ApplicationStartingEvent`, `ApplicationEnvironmentPreparedEvent`, `ApplicationContextInitializedEvent`, `ApplicationPreparedEvent`, `ContextRefreshedEvent`, `ApplicationStartedEvent` (context refreshed, runners not yet called), `AvailabilityChangeEvent` (liveness correct), `ApplicationReadyEvent` (after all `CommandLineRunner` and `ApplicationRunner` beans have run; readiness accepting traffic), and `ApplicationFailedEvent` on a start-up error.

Ordering rules appear in several places and are often confused. `@Order`, `Ordered` and `@Priority` sort collections injected as `List<T>`, listeners, filters registered as beans, and post-processors; they do **not** control the order in which beans are created. Creation order follows dependencies and `@DependsOn`.

### Worked example

The first listing is a complete plain-JDK container, about a hundred lines, that implements the algorithm described above: bean definitions, constructor instantiation by reflection, field injection of an `@Inject` annotation, a `BeanPostProcessor` list, `@PostConstruct`, and the three-level cache for a deliberate cycle. It is not Spring code, but each method corresponds to a Spring method named in the comments.

blocks.text: The second listing is the Spring Boot equivalent used to observe every callback of one bean in a real container, together with a `BeanPostProcessor` and a `BeanFactoryPostProcessor`.

blocks.text:
### Hands-on

The plain-JDK container was compiled and run on the build machine (JDK 21, `java MiniContainer.java`). The output demonstrates the three-level cache: `paymentService` is created while `orderService` is still in creation, receives the early reference, and is completed first.

blocks.code:
$ java MiniContainer.java
create 'orderService'
  [instantiate] OrderService
  [inject] orderService.payments <- 'paymentService'
create 'paymentService'
  [instantiate] PaymentService
  [inject] paymentService.orders <- 'orderService'
  [cache] early reference for 'orderService' promoted from level 3 to level 2
  [BPP.before] paymentService
  [@PostConstruct] PaymentService
  [BPP.after]  paymentService
  [BPP.before] orderService
  [@PostConstruct] OrderService
  [BPP.after]  orderService
order placed, payment charged
same instance: true
blocks.title: Output of the mini container (real run)

blocks.text:
What to notice: the `@PostConstruct` of `paymentService` runs **before** that of `orderService`, although `orderService` was requested first. A bean is initialised when its own population is complete, which for the inner bean of a cycle occurs earlier. Code in `@PostConstruct` must therefore not assume that the beans it depends on in a cycle have finished initialising.

Running `LifecycleProbe` in a Boot application produces the following sequence; the output is typical and was not run on the build machine, since no Spring artifacts are available there.

blocks.code:
BFPP   definitions=24 probe.scope=singleton
1 constructor
2 BeanNameAware probe
3 ApplicationContextAware
BPP    before-init
4 @PostConstruct
5 afterPropertiesSet
6 initMethod
BPP    after-init
... application started ...
7 @PreDestroy
8 DisposableBean.destroy
9 destroyMethod
blocks.title: typical output (not run on the build machine)

blocks.text:
The line order of 3, `BPP before-init` and 4 reflects that `ApplicationContextAwareProcessor` and `CommonAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` are themselves `BeanPostProcessor` instances that run ahead of the user-defined one by order. The exact count of definitions depends on the auto-configuration present. To inspect definitions of a running application, `GET /actuator/beans` (when the `beans` endpoint is exposed) lists every bean, its scope, its type and its dependencies.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 1: application fails at start-up with a circular dependency

**Scenario.** A service `InvoiceService` was extended to send notifications. `NotificationService` already depended on `InvoiceService` to load invoice data. After the change the application no longer starts.

**Symptoms.** The log ends with:

blocks.code:
***************************
APPLICATION FAILED TO START
***************************

Description:

The dependencies of some of the beans in the application context form a cycle:

┌─────┐
|  invoiceService defined in file [.../InvoiceService.class]
↑     ↓
|  notificationService defined in file [.../NotificationService.class]
└─────┘

Action:

Relying upon circular references is discouraged and they are prohibited by default.
Update your application to remove the dependency cycle between beans. As a last resort,
it may be possible to break the cycle automatically by setting
spring.main.allow-circular-references to true.

blocks.text:
**Diagnosis.** The failure analyser (`BeanCurrentlyInCreationFailureAnalyzer`) prints the cycle and each class. The cycle can also be confirmed with the Actuator `beans` endpoint on a variant that runs with `spring.main.allow-circular-references=true`, which lists the `dependencies` array of both beans. Constructor injection on at least one side confirms that the cycle is not resolvable even with the flag enabled.

**Root cause.** Both services require each other during construction. The flag change in Spring Boot 2.6 turned a previously tolerated design fault into a start-up failure.

**Fix.** Break the cycle by design, in this order of preference: (1) extract the shared logic into a third bean, `InvoiceQueries`, that both services use; (2) invert the dependency with an event, `InvoiceIssuedEvent`, published by `InvoiceService` and consumed by a listener in `NotificationService`; (3) as a last resort, mark one injection point `@Lazy`, which injects a proxy that resolves the target on first use.

blocks.title: NotificationService.java

blocks.text:
**Prevention.** Keep the property at its default of `false`. Review dependency direction (controllers to services to repositories) and fail the build on cycles with an architecture test.

#### Problem 2: the wrong implementation is injected

**Scenario.** Two beans implement `PaymentGateway`: `StripeGateway` and `SandboxGateway`. A new `CheckoutService` receives `SandboxGateway` in production.

**Symptoms.** Either start-up fails with `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException: expected single matching bean but` `found 2`, or, worse, start-up succeeds and the wrong implementation is used.

**Diagnosis.** `GET /actuator/beans` filtered for the interface type shows both candidates. The resolution algorithm in `DefaultListableBeanFactory.determineAutowireCandidate` applies, in order: a `@Primary` candidate, the candidate with the highest `@Priority`, and finally a match of the injection point's parameter or field **name** against a bean name. The silent selection happened through the last rule: the constructor parameter was named `sandboxGateway`. **Root cause.** Name-based fallback matches hide ambiguity. A refactoring that renames the parameter changes behaviour.

**Fix.** State the intent explicitly with `@Qualifier("stripeGateway")` at the injection point, or mark the production bean `@Primary`. For default-with-override designs, Spring Framework 6.2 offers `@Fallback`. Use `@Profile("!prod")` to keep the sandbox bean out of production.

**Prevention.** Inject `List<PaymentGateway>` or `Map<String, PaymentGateway>` when selection is a runtime decision, and avoid several beans of one type without a qualifier.

blocks.text:
#### Problem 3: start-up takes more than a minute

**Scenario.** A service with 400 beans needs 70 seconds to become ready, which makes rolling deployments slow and probe configuration fragile.

**Symptoms.** Log timestamps show a long gap between "Starting" and "Started". Container start-up is fast on a developer laptop and slow in a CPU-limited pod.

**Diagnosis.** (1) Set `logging.level.org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure=DEBUG` or run with `--debug` to confirm the number of auto-configurations that matched. (2) Attach a `BufferingApplicationStartup(2048)` through `SpringApplication.setApplicationStartup(...)` and expose the Actuator `startup` endpoint (`GET` `/actuator/startup`), which returns timed steps such as `spring.beans.instantiate` with the bean name. (3) Sort by duration to find the slowest beans. Typical findings are beans that open a remote connection in `@PostConstruct`, Hibernate schema validation, a Flyway migration, and a very wide `@ComponentScan`.

**Root cause.** Eager instantiation of all singletons does expensive work serially on the main thread. A CPU limit of 0.5 core further lengthens the class-loading and reflection work.

**Fix.** Move remote work out of `@PostConstruct` (initialise lazily or on `ApplicationReadyEvent`), narrow `@ComponentScan`, and consider `spring.main.lazy-initialization=true`. Lazy initialisation defers failures from start-up to the first request and delays the first request's latency, so it is applied selectively with `@Lazy` on heavy beans rather than globally in production. For the larger options (class data sharing, AOT, native image) see the chapter on performance tuning.

**Prevention.** Record start-up time in CI from the `startup` endpoint and fail on regressions.

blocks.text:
### Questions to expect

1. **What is the difference between BeanFactory and ApplicationContext?** `BeanFactory` is the basic container contract (definition registry, `getBean`, lazy creation). `ApplicationContext` adds eager singleton creation, events, message sources, resource loading, environment and automatic post-processor detection. In practice the application always uses an `ApplicationContext`, which delegates to a `DefaultListableBeanFactory`.
2. **What happens inside refresh()?** The definitions are loaded and post-processed (`BeanFactoryPostProcessor`, `ConfigurationClassPostProcessor`), `BeanPostProcessor` beans are registered, the web server is created in `onRefresh`, non-lazy singletons are created in `finishBeanFactoryInitialization`, and `finishRefresh` starts lifecycle beans and publishes `ContextRefreshedEvent`.
3. **Explain BeanFactoryPostProcessor versus BeanPostProcessor.** The first modifies metadata before instances exist; the second wraps or modifies instances around initialisation. AOP proxies come from a `BeanPostProcessor`.
4. **In which order are callbacks invoked on a bean?** Constructor, injection, Aware callbacks, `@PostConstruct`, `afterPropertiesSet`, custom init method, `postProcessAfterInitialization` (proxying); on shutdown `@PreDestroy`, `destroy`, custom destroy method.
5. **How does Spring resolve circular dependencies?** For singletons with setter or field injection, through the three-level cache: an early reference is exposed through an `ObjectFactory` before population. Constructor cycles cannot be resolved. Since Boot 2.6 the feature is off by default.
6. **Why does a request-scoped bean in a singleton need a proxy?** The singleton is constructed once; the proxy resolves the correct target per call from the scope.
7. **What is the difference between full and lite** `@Configuration`**?** Full mode subclasses the class with CGLIB so that inter-`@Bean` calls return the singleton; lite mode (`proxyBeanMethods = false`) performs plain calls and is faster.
8. **Are Spring events asynchronous?** No, by default they run synchronously on the publisher's thread, including participation in the publisher's transaction.
9. **Does** `@Order` **determine bean creation order?** No. It orders collections and listeners; creation order follows dependencies and `@DependsOn`.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Metadata (`BeanDefinition`), definition post-processing (`BeanFactoryPostProcessor`) and instance decoration (`BeanPostProcessor`) are separate stages of `refresh()`.
- Proxies are created in `postProcessAfterInitialization`; the exposed bean may differ from the constructed object.
- Circular references work only for singletons with field or setter injection through the three-level cache, and are disabled by default since Boot 2.6.
- Full `@Configuration` mode uses CGLIB to preserve singleton semantics between `@Bean` calls; lite mode does not.
- Events are synchronous by default; `@Order` sorts collections, not creation.
- Ambiguity is resolved by qualifier, `@Primary`, `@Priority`, then parameter name; state intent explicitly.

Transactions, asynchronous execution, caching, retries, method security, metrics and logging share one property: each is behaviour that must run around a method call without being part of the method's business logic. Writing that behaviour inside every service method duplicates code and couples the domain to infrastructure. Aspect-oriented programming (AOP) separates it: the behaviour is declared once and applied to many methods by a rule. In Spring, the mechanism is almost always a **proxy**, an object that stands in front of the real bean and intercepts calls. Understanding proxies explains, in a single model, why `@Transactional`, `@Async`, `@Cacheable`, `@Retryable` and `@PreAuthorize` all fail in exactly the same situations.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Vocabulary

rows: A module that holds cross-cutting logic, declared with @Aspect on a Spring bean.
A point in program execution. Spring AOP supports only **method execution** on Spring beans.
A predicate that selects join points, written in AspectJ pointcut syntax (execution, within, @annotation, args, bean).
The action taken at a join point: @Before, @AfterReturning, @AfterThrowing, @After, @Around.
Spring's pairing of one Advice and one Pointcut. Every @Transactional or @Async facility is an advisor.
The object created by the framework that applies the advisors and delegates to the target.
blocks.caption: AOP terms as used by Spring.

blocks.text:
Spring AOP is not AspectJ. AspectJ modifies bytecode at compile time or load time and can advise field access, constructors and calls made from `this`. Spring AOP only builds runtime proxies. It borrows the AspectJ **annotation and** **pointcut language** (through the `aspectjweaver` library) but not its weaving. This choice explains every limitation listed later.

#### How a proxy gets into the application

The proxy is created by a `BeanPostProcessor`. When `spring-boot-starter-aop` is present, `AopAutoConfiguration` enables `AnnotationAwareAspectJAutoProxyCreator`. In `postProcessAfterInitialization` it collects every advisor in the context (beans annotated `@Aspect`, plus infrastructure advisors such as `BeanFactoryTransactionAttributeSourceAdvisor`), tests each advisor's pointcut against the bean's class, and, if any match, wraps the bean with `ProxyFactory`. The context then stores the **proxy** in `singletonObjects`, so every consumer that injects the type receives the proxy and the raw object remains reachable only from inside the proxy.

Two proxy technologies exist.

rows: The target implements at least one interface
A non-final class with a visible constructor
java.lang.reflect.Proxy generates a class implementing the interfaces; InvocationHandler.invoke dispatches
A generated **subclass** of the target overrides methods and calls the interceptors; the instance is created without invoking the constructor (Objenesis)
Possible, because the proxy is a subclass
Final classes cannot be proxied; final methods are not intercepted

blocks.text:
Spring Boot defaults to class-based (CGLIB) proxies even for beans with interfaces, because injection by implementation class then works. A plain Spring Framework application created without Boot defaults to JDK proxies when interfaces exist.

#### Advice types and the interceptor chain

All advice is converted into `MethodInterceptor` objects. When a method is called on the proxy, the proxy builds a `ReflectiveMethodInvocation` that holds the ordered list of interceptors for that method and calls `proceed()`. Each interceptor either calls `proceed()` to continue (the next interceptor, or finally the target method through reflection) or returns early. This recursion is why advice nests like parentheses: the first interceptor is outermost.

rows: Runs before the method. Cannot prevent execution except by throwing an exception.
Runs after a normal return; can bind the return value.
Runs after an exception; can bind the exception. The exception continues to propagate.
Receives a ProceedingJoinPoint, controls whether and when proceed() is called, and may change arguments and result. All others can be expressed through it.
blocks.caption: Advice types.

blocks.text: Use the weakest advice that suffices. `@Around` is powerful and has one recurring defect: forgetting to return the value of `proceed()`, which silently makes every advised method return `null`.

blocks.text:
#### Pointcut expressions

The most used designators are:

rows: `execution(public * com.example.library..*Service.*(..)): public` `methods of classes named *Service in the package and subpackages`
`within(com.example.library.web..*): all methods of types in the` `package`
`args(String, ..): methods whose first argument is a String`
blocks.caption: Pointcut designators (from the Spring Framework reference).

blocks.text:
Pointcuts can be named with `@Pointcut` methods and combined with `&&`, `||` and `!`. Evaluation happens twice: statically when the post-processor decides whether to wrap the class, and, for `args` and `@annotation` binding, dynamically at call time. Pointcuts that cover many beans slow down start-up, because each pointcut is tested against each bean class.

#### Transactions, asynchronous execution, caching and retry are proxies

The annotations used in the data and service layers are implemented as advisors that follow the same chain model.

rows: AnnotationAsyncExecutionInterceptor submits the call to an AsyncTaskExecutor
RetryOperationsInterceptor (spring-retry library; Framework 7 integrates retry into the core)
blocks.caption: Built-in facilities implemented with proxies.

blocks.text: Because they share one mechanism, they share every limitation, and they stack. A method that carries both `@Transactional` and `@Cacheable` passes through two interceptors whose relative order is controlled by the `order` attribute of the `@Enable...` annotations (both default to lowest precedence, which means the order between them is not guaranteed unless stated).

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Advice methods inside **one** aspect class are ordered since Spring Framework 5.2.7 as Around, Before, After, AfterReturning, AfterThrowing on the way in. Between **different** aspects, the `@Order` value (or the `Ordered` interface) decides; lower numbers have higher precedence. Without an order the sequence is undefined.

#### Limitations of proxy-based AOP

1. **Self-invocation.** A call to `this.method()` inside the target bypasses the proxy, because `this` is the raw object. No advice runs.
2. **Final classes and methods** cannot be overridden by a CGLIB subclass. A final method invoked on the proxy runs on the proxy instance, whose fields were never initialised (the instance was created without the constructor), which produces `NullPointerException` or silently incorrect values.
3. **Private methods** are never intercepted. Since Spring Framework 6.0, class-based proxies also advise protected and package-visible methods for transactions and similar annotations; private methods remain unsupported.
4. **Objects not managed by Spring** (created with `new`) have no proxy.
5. **Early use.** A bean used during initialisation of a `BeanPostProcessor` is created before the auto-proxy creator exists and is therefore not advised.

blocks.text:
### Worked example

The scenario is a library service whose borrow operation must be audited, timed, and transactional. The code uses Spring Boot 3.x with `spring-boot-starter-aop`. Each file is shown in full.

blocks.title: Timed.java
TimingAspect.java
AuditAspect.java
LoanService.java

blocks.text:
What to notice: `borrow` is advised by three interceptors (audit, timing, transaction) because all three pointcuts match; the call to `writeAudit` inside the same class is not advised at all, so `REQUIRES_NEW` has no effect (see Problem 1).

### Hands-on

The self-invocation defect and the chain order can be reproduced with plain JDK dynamic proxies, which are the same technology as `JdkDynamicAopProxy`. The program below places an advice that stands for `TransactionInterceptor` around a service whose `transfer` method calls its own `audit` method.

blocks.title: SelfInvocation.java

blocks.code:
$ java SelfInvocation.java
1. call through one proxy:
  [tx] before transfer
    transfer A -> B
    audit: transfer done
  [tx] after  transfer
2. chain of two proxies (outer = first advice):
  [outer] before audit
  [inner] before audit
    audit: direct call
  [inner] after  audit
  [outer] after  audit
3. proxy class facts:
  class = $Proxy0
  is subclass of impl? false
  interfaces = [interface SelfInvocation$AccountService]
blocks.title: Real run on the build machine (JDK 21)

blocks.text:
Section 1 shows the defect: `[tx] before` appears once, for `transfer`, and nothing appears around the nested `audit`. Section 2 shows the nesting order of a chain: before-advice in order, after-advice in reverse. Section 3 shows why a JDK proxy cannot be cast to the implementation class.

The final-method limitation of class-based proxies is reproduced by writing the subclass by hand, which is what CGLIB generates at runtime.

blocks.title: FinalMethodProxy.java

blocks.code:
$ java FinalMethodProxy.java
  [advice] before open
open():  open by alice
close(): close by null
blocks.title: Real run on the build machine (JDK 21)

blocks.text:
`close()` executes on the proxy instance, whose field `owner` is `null`, and no advice runs. The same effect in Spring appears as a `NullPointerException` in a final method that uses an injected field.

Running the library application with the aspects above produces the following output for one borrow request. The output is typical and was not run on the build machine.

blocks.code:
INFO  c.e.library.aop.TimingAspect : loan.borrow took 14 ms on thread http-nio-8080-exec-2
INFO  c.e.library.aop.AuditAspect  : audit ok: LoanService.borrow(..) -> Loan[id=17, ...]
blocks.title: typical output (not run on the build machine)

blocks.text:
The audit line follows the timing line because `AuditAspect` (order 1) is outermost: its after-returning advice executes after the timing advice has already finished. To confirm that a bean is proxied at runtime, evaluate `AopUtils.isAopProxy(bean)` or print `bean.getClass()`, which shows a name of the form `LoanService$$SpringCGLIB$$0`.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 1: @Transactional ignored on an internal call

**Scenario.** `borrow` must always write an audit row, even when the surrounding business transaction rolls back. The audit method was declared `REQUIRES_NEW` so that it commits independently. In production a failed borrow leaves no audit row.

**Symptoms.** The audit table lacks rows for failed borrows. Unit tests that call `writeAudit` directly pass. SQL logs show only one transaction per request.

**Diagnosis.** (1) Enable `logging.level.org.springframework.transaction.interceptor=TRACE`; the log shows `Getting transaction for [LoanService.borrow]` and no line for `writeAudit`. (2) Enable `logging.level.org.springframework.jdbc.datasource.DataSourceTransactionManager=DEBUG` (or `JpaTransactionManager`) and count `Creating new transaction` lines: one appears where two were expected. (3) Print `AopUtils.isAopProxy(this)` inside `borrow`: it returns `false`, because `this` is the raw object. **Root cause.** `borrow` calls `writeAudit` through `this`. The proxy, which holds the `TransactionInterceptor`, is bypassed (see the self-invocation limitation).

**Fix.** Move `writeAudit` to a separate bean so that the call crosses a proxy boundary.

blocks.title: AuditWriter.java

blocks.text:
`LoanService` then injects `AuditWriter` and calls `audit.write(loan.id(), "BORROWED")`. Alternatives, in decreasing order of preference: inject the bean into itself with `@Lazy` (`@Autowired @Lazy LoanService self;`), which keeps the code in one class but obscures the design; use `AopContext.currentProxy()` with `@EnableAspectJAutoProxy(exposeProxy = true)`, which couples the code to Spring AOP; or switch to AspectJ weaving mode (`@EnableTransactionManagement(mode = AdviceMode.ASPECTJ)`), which requires a weaver at compile or load time.

**Prevention.** Keep annotated methods that are called only internally to a minimum, and write a slice or integration test that asserts the number of transactions (`TransactionSynchronizationManager.isActualTransactionActive()`) or the persisted audit row.

blocks.text:
#### Problem 2: @Async method runs on the request thread

**Scenario.** `ReportService.generate()` was annotated `@Async` to free the request thread, yet the endpoint still takes eight seconds.

**Symptoms.** The log line printed inside the method shows `http-nio-8080-exec-3` instead of `task-1`. Response time equals the processing time.

**Diagnosis.** Check the thread name in a log statement inside the method. Check that `@EnableAsync` is present on a configuration class, that the method is called from **another** bean, and that the method is not `private` or `final`. Print `Thread.currentThread().getName()` at both the call site and inside the method.

**Root cause.** Either `@EnableAsync` is missing (no `AsyncAnnotationBeanPostProcessor`, so no proxy), or the method is called from another method of the same class (self-invocation). **Fix.** Add `@EnableAsync` to a `@Configuration` class, call the method from a different bean, and declare an executor explicitly so that the pool is bounded:

blocks.title: AsyncConfig.java

blocks.text:
The annotated method is then `@Async("reportExecutor")` and returns `void` or `CompletableFuture<T>`. An exception thrown from a `void` async method is not visible to the caller and goes to the `AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler`; a `CompletableFuture` return type propagates it through the future.

**Prevention.** Log the thread name in a start-up test of each async method. Name and bound the executor explicitly instead of relying on implicit defaults.

#### Problem 3: NullPointerException in a final method of a proxied bean

**Scenario.** After adding `@Transactional` to a class, a helper method `String describe()` that returns a value computed from an injected field starts to throw `NullPointerException` in production only through the controller.

**Symptoms.** The stack trace points into the method body, at an injected field. The same method works in a unit test constructed with `new`.

**Diagnosis.** The method is declared `final` (or the class is a Kotlin class without the `kotlin-spring` plugin, where classes are final by default). Inspect `bean.getClass()` at the injection site: the name contains `$$SpringCGLIB$$`, which confirms a class-based proxy. The stack trace shows no `CglibAopProxy` frame for the failing call.

**Root cause.** The CGLIB subclass cannot override a final method, so the call executes on the proxy instance, whose fields were never populated.

**Fix.** Remove `final` from methods of proxied classes, or extract the helper into a non-proxied utility.

**Prevention.** Avoid `final` on public methods of Spring beans that carry advice; configure the `kotlin-spring` compiler plugin for Kotlin.

### Questions to expect

1. **How does Spring implement** `@Transactional`**?** A `BeanPostProcessor` (the auto-proxy creator) wraps beans that match the `BeanFactoryTransactionAttributeSourceAdvisor` pointcut. The proxy's `TransactionInterceptor` obtains a transaction from the `PlatformTransactionManager` before invoking the target, and commits or rolls back afterwards.
2. **JDK proxy versus CGLIB?** A JDK proxy implements the target's interfaces through `java.lang.reflect.Proxy`; CGLIB generates a subclass. Spring Boot defaults to CGLIB (`spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true`).
3. **Why does** `@Transactional` **not work when a method calls another method of the same class?** The internal call uses `this`, which is the raw target, so the proxy is bypassed. Call through another bean, or restructure.
4. **Which methods can be advised?** Public methods on Spring-managed beans always; protected and package-visible methods with class-based proxies since Spring 6.0; never private, static or final.
5. **Spring AOP versus AspectJ?** Spring AOP uses runtime proxies and supports method execution on Spring beans. AspectJ weaves bytecode and supports field access, constructors, and self-invocation.
6. **How is the order of two aspects defined?** By `@Order` or `Ordered`; the lower value is the outer interceptor. Without an order the sequence is undefined.
7. **What is the difference between** `@Before` **and** `@Around`**?** `@Around` controls whether the method proceeds and can transform arguments and result; `@Before` cannot stop execution except by throwing.
8. **Why can an advised bean not be created with** `new`**?** Only container-managed beans pass through the post-processor, so only they are proxied.
9. **What does** `@Async` **return and where do exceptions go?** `void` or `Future`/`CompletableFuture`. Exceptions in void methods go to the `AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler`.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Spring AOP is proxy-based: a `BeanPostProcessor` replaces the bean with a JDK proxy (interfaces) or a CGLIB subclass (Boot default).
- `@Transactional`, `@Async`, `@Cacheable`, `@Retryable` and method security are advisors; they all fail on self-invocation, on private, static and final methods, and on objects created with `new`.
- Interceptors nest like parentheses; `@Order` (lower is outer) decides between aspects.
- Fix self-invocation by calling across a bean boundary; the proxy must be on the call path.
- Verify with `AopUtils.isAopProxy`, the class name containing `$$SpringCGLIB$$`, and TRACE logging of the interceptor packages.

Spring Boot reduces a hundred lines of infrastructure wiring to the presence of a dependency on the classpath. The reduction is not magic: it is a list of candidate configuration classes, each guarded by conditions that inspect the classpath, the existing beans and the environment. A developer who understands the list, the conditions and the binding of properties can answer the two questions that dominate production work: "why did Boot create this bean?" and "why did Boot ignore my setting?".

### Concept and mechanism

#### Anatomy of @SpringBootApplication

`@SpringBootApplication` is a composed annotation with three responsibilities.

- `@SpringBootConfiguration` (a specialisation of `@Configuration`) marks the class as a source of bean definitions and lets tests locate it.
- `@ComponentScan` scans the package of the annotated class and its subpackages. It carries two exclude filters, `TypeExcludeFilter` (used by test slices) and `AutoConfigurationExcludeFilter` (prevents auto-configuration classes from being picked up by scanning).
- `@EnableAutoConfiguration` is itself composed of `@AutoConfigurationPackage`, which records the base package for later use (for example by Spring Data to find entities and repositories), and `@Import(AutoConfigurationImportSelector.class)`.

The consequence of the first two points is a classical defect: a class located **outside** the package tree of the main class is not scanned, so its beans do not exist. Setting `scanBasePackages` or moving the main class to the root package corrects it.

#### From the imports file to bean definitions

`AutoConfigurationImportSelector` is a `DeferredImportSelector`: it is processed after all user `@Configuration` classes, which guarantees that `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` can see user-defined beans. It reads the file `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports` from every jar on the classpath, one fully qualified class name per line. The `spring-boot-autoconfigure` jar alone lists more than a hundred classes. (Before Boot 2.7 the list was registered in `spring.factories` under the key `EnableAutoConfiguration`; Boot 3.0 removed that mechanism for auto-configuration.)

The selector applies three filters before any class is parsed:

1. Names listed in `exclude` or `excludeName` of `@EnableAutoConfiguration`, or in the property `spring.autoconfigure.exclude`, are removed.
2. `AutoConfigurationImportFilter` implementations (`OnClassCondition`, `OnBeanCondition`, `OnWebApplicationCondition`) evaluate the cheap conditions using pre-computed metadata in `META-INF/spring-autoconfigure-metadata.properties`, so that classes whose required library is absent are dropped without being loaded.
3. The survivors are sorted by `@AutoConfigureOrder`, `@AutoConfigureBefore`/`@AutoConfigureAfter` (or the `before` and `after` attributes of `@AutoConfiguration`). Ordering only affects the **registration order of bean definitions**; instantiation order still follows dependencies.

The remaining classes are parsed like ordinary configuration classes, and each `@Conditional` on a class or `@Bean` method is evaluated at parse or registration time.

blocks.text: #### The condition annotations

rows: Whether a class is present on the classpath. On a @Bean method use the name attribute (strings), because a class literal would be loaded while reading the annotation.
Whether a bean of a type, name or annotation exists. Intended for auto-configuration classes, which run after user beans.
A property by prefix, name, havingValue and matchIfMissing. Without havingValue any value other than false matches.
Servlet, reactive or any web application type.
Presence of a resource such as a file on the classpath.
A SpEL expression. Referencing beans in it forces early initialisation.

blocks.caption: Frequently used conditions (Spring Boot 3.x).

blocks.text:
Two design rules follow from the mechanism. First, every bean definition in an auto-configuration should carry `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`, so that an application can replace it by declaring its own bean of the same type; the library's bean then **backs off**. Second, give the `@Bean` method the most specific return type available: bean conditions inspect the declared return type before the method runs.

#### Property binding and relaxed binding

Typed configuration is bound by `ConfigurationPropertiesBindingPostProcessor` using the `Binder`. A class annotated `@ConfigurationProperties("audit")` is registered either with `@EnableConfigurationProperties(AuditProperties.class)` or through `@ConfigurationPropertiesScan`. Binding sources are all `PropertySource` objects of the `Environment`. Java records and classes with a single parameterised constructor use **constructor binding** automatically in Boot 3; mutable beans use setters. `@Validated` activates Jakarta Bean Validation on the bound object, so an invalid value fails at start-up instead of at first use.

Relaxed binding means a property can be written in several spellings for the same canonical key. The canonical form used for lookup and in documentation is lower-case kebab-case separated by dots (`audit.slow-threshold`).

rows: Camel case and underscore notation are also accepted.
Replace dots with underscores, remove dashes, upper case.

blocks.text:
#### Externalised configuration order

Spring Boot merges many property sources and the **last source wins**. The reference lists them from lowest to highest priority. The sources that matter in everyday work are, in ascending order:

1. Defaults set with `SpringApplication.setDefaultProperties`.
2. `@PropertySource` annotations (loaded late: too late for `logging.*` and `spring.main.*`).
3. Config data: `application.properties` and `application.yml`, then profile-specific `application-{profile}` files. Within the config data, files outside the jar override files inside the jar, and profile-specific files override non-specific ones. The default search locations, in ascending order, are `classpath:/`, `classpath:/config/`, `file:./`, `file:./config/` and `file:./config/*/`.
4. OS environment variables.
5. Java system properties (`-D`).
6. `SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON` / `spring.application.json`.
7. Command-line arguments (`--server.port=9090`).
8. In tests: the `properties` attribute of `@SpringBootTest`, `@DynamicPropertySource`, and `@TestPropertySource`.

blocks.text:
`spring.config.location` **replaces** the default search locations, while `spring.config.additional-location` adds locations that take precedence over the defaults. `spring.config.import` pulls in further files or sources (`optional:file:./local.yml`, `configtree:/run/secrets/`, `env:MY_JSON`) and the imported values override those of the importing file. Profiles are activated with `spring.profiles.active`, grouped with `spring.profiles.group.prod=proddb,prodmq`, and used inside a multi-document YAML file with `spring.config.activate.on-profile`. The legacy `bootstrap` context is not used in Boot 3 unless the `spring-cloud-starter-bootstrap` dependency is added.

#### Secrets

Secrets must not be committed to the repository or baked into the image. Acceptable sources, in increasing order of maturity: environment variables injected by the platform; files mounted from a secret store and read with `spring.config.import=optional:configtree:/run/secrets/` (each file name becomes a key and the file content the value, which suits Kubernetes secrets); and an external secret manager reached through a Spring Cloud integration. The Actuator `env` and `configprops` endpoints mask values by default since Boot 3.0 (`management.endpoint.env.show-values` defaults to `never`), and must still be protected, because key names and origins are exposed.

### Worked example

The worked example is a custom starter, `audit-spring-boot-starter`, that provides an `AuditLogger` bean. It consists of two modules, following the naming convention in the reference: an `audit-spring-boot-autoconfigure` module containing code and configuration, and an empty `audit-spring-boot-starter` module that depends on it. (The name of a third-party module must not begin with `spring-boot`.)

What to notice: no test starts a web server or scans packages; the five tests cover each decision point of the auto-configuration (default creation, binding, back-off, property switch, validation).

The mechanism that decides each of these outcomes can be modelled in plain Java. The following program keeps user beans first, then evaluates an ordered list of candidates with conditions, and prints a report in the style of the Boot condition report. The candidates use a real class-presence check (`Class.forName`), a property check, and a missing-bean check.

blocks.title: MiniAutoConfig.java

$ java MiniAutoConfig.java
Positive matches: [simpleRegistry]
Negative matches:
  systemClock: did not match, @ConditionalOnMissingBean(Clock2)
  prometheusRegistry: did not match, @ConditionalOnClass(io.prometheus.client.CollectorRegistry)
  debugEndpoint: did not match, @ConditionalOnProperty(app.debug=true)
Beans: {userClock=FixedClock2[], simpleRegistry=MetricsRegistry[backend=simple]}
blocks.title: Real run on the build machine (JDK 21)

blocks.text:
The result mirrors the real behaviour: the user's clock suppresses `systemClock`; the first registry candidate fails on a missing class; the second matches because the first did not register a bean (`@ConditionalOnMissingBean` is order-sensitive).

### Hands-on

An application that includes the starter and sets `audit.prefix=SEC` in `application.yml` can be asked to explain itself. Starting it with `--debug` (or `debug=true`) prints the condition evaluation report. The output below is the typical shape of the report for the audit starter (not run on the build machine).

$ curl -s localhost:8080/actuator/conditions | jq '.contexts[].positiveMatches | keys[]' | head -3
$ curl -s localhost:8080/actuator/configprops/audit
$ curl -s localhost:8080/actuator/env/audit.prefix
blocks.title: typical commands (not run on the build machine)

blocks.text:
`/actuator/env/audit.prefix` lists every property source that defines the key in precedence order, with the origin (file and line) of the winning value, which settles most disputes about "which file won".

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 1: a property is set but the value is not applied

**Scenario.** `audit.slowThreshold: 2s` was added to `application.yml` and the service still warns about 600 ms operations.

**Symptoms.** The bean shows the default of 500 ms; there is no error, because an unbound but spelled-differently property is simply an unknown key.

**Diagnosis.** (1) `GET /actuator/configprops/audit` shows the bound values and confirms the effective `slowThreshold`. (2) `GET /actuator/env/audit.slow-threshold` lists the property sources that define the canonical key; an empty result means the key never reached the `Environment`. (3) `logging.level.org.springframework.boot.context.config=TRACE` prints every config file candidate that was loaded or skipped. Typical causes found this way: the file sits in `src/test/resources` or is not copied to the jar; it is named `application.yaml` and `application.yml` at once; a `spring.config.location` entry replaced the default locations; a profile-specific file is not active; the YAML indent places the key under another prefix.

When a value is found but invalid, the failure analyser prints a structured explanation (typical text):

blocks.code:
APPLICATION FAILED TO START
Description:
Failed to bind properties under 'audit' to com.example.audit.AuditProperties:
    Property: audit.slow-threshold
    Value: "2 secs"
    Origin: class path resource [application.yml] - 4:19
    Reason: failed to convert java.lang.String to java.time.Duration
Action:
Update your application's configuration

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** In the scenario the key was written under the wrong parent (`audit.slow-threshold` placed under `spring:`), so it was a different key.

**Fix.** Correct the nesting. Use the Duration formats `2s`, `500ms`, `PT2S` or the ISO-8601 form; `2 secs` is invalid.

**Prevention.** Add `spring-boot-configuration-processor` to the autoconfigure module as an annotation processor so that IDEs flag unknown keys; use `@Validated` for constraints; and in tests assert the bound object.

#### Problem 2: an auto-configured bean is missing or has been replaced

**Scenario.** After a team declared a `DataSource` bean for a second database, the application's HikariCP settings under `spring.datasource.hikari.*` stopped having any effect, and the Actuator `metrics` no longer showed the `hikaricp.*` series.

**Symptoms.** Properties are ignored without a message; the pool shows default values.

**Diagnosis.** Run with `--debug` and search for `DataSourceAutoConfiguration` in the negative matches: `@ConditionalOnMissingBean (types: javax.sql.DataSource; SearchStrategy: all) found beans` `'secondaryDataSource'`. This line is the definitive explanation: the application bean made the auto-configuration back off. `GET /actuator/beans` confirms that only the user-defined `DataSource` exists.

**Root cause.** Auto-configuration is a default, not a mandate. The user-defined bean replaced the auto-configured one, and the user-defined bean never read the `spring.datasource.*` properties.

**Fix.** Create each data source explicitly and bind the properties explicitly:

blocks.title: DataSourceConfig.java

blocks.text:
**Prevention.** Treat any user-declared bean of an infrastructure type (`DataSource`, `ObjectMapper`, `RestTemplate`, `TransactionManager`) as a decision to own that type's configuration, and keep the condition report in the diagnostic toolkit.

#### Problem 3: the wrong value wins in production

**Scenario.** `server.port` is 8080 in `application.yml` and 8443 in `application-prod.yml`. The production container listens on 9000.

**Symptoms.** The port differs from both files.

**Diagnosis.** `GET /actuator/env/server.port` (or the `env` endpoint output) lists sources in precedence order: `systemEnvironment: SERVER_PORT=9000`, then `applicationConfig: [classpath:/application-prod.yml]`, then the base file. The environment variable defined in the deployment manifest wins over both files.

**Root cause.** The precedence rules were not applied: OS environment variables override config data. The manifest had been copied from another service.

**Fix.** Remove the stale variable, or make the intent explicit. Keep a single authoritative place per setting.

**Prevention.** Document the intended source of each deployment-specific setting and print the winning origin during start-up checks. Do not rely on overriding the same key in many layers.

### Questions to expect

1. **What does** `@SpringBootApplication` **consist of?** `@SpringBootConfiguration`, `@EnableAutoConfiguration` and `@ComponentScan` with two filters.
2. **How does auto-configuration find its classes?** `AutoConfigurationImportSelector` reads `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports` from all jars (`spring.factories` before Boot 2.7), filters by `OnClassCondition` metadata, orders the rest and imports them as deferred configuration.
3. **How can an application override an auto-configured bean?** Declare a bean of the same type; the auto-configured bean's `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` condition fails and it backs off.
4. **How is the reason for a missing bean found?** Start with `--debug` or call `/actuator/conditions` and search the negative matches.
5. **What is relaxed binding?** Several spellings of a key map to one canonical kebab-case name; environment variables use upper case with underscores and no dashes.
6. **What is the order of property sources?** Defaults, `@PropertySource`, config data (jar, then outside the jar, with profile files after non-profile files), environment variables, system properties, JSON, command line, test sources; the last wins.
7. `@Value` **versus** `@ConfigurationProperties`**?** `@Value` injects a single expression, matches relaxed forms only when the canonical kebab-case name is used in the placeholder, and offers no validation or metadata; `@ConfigurationProperties` binds a typed, validated structure with relaxed rules and IDE metadata.
8. **How is a custom starter built?** An autoconfigure module with `@AutoConfiguration` classes, an `.imports` file, `@ConfigurationProperties` and conditions, plus a starter module that only declares dependencies.
9. **How are secrets supplied safely?** Environment variables, mounted secret files imported with `configtree:`, or a secret manager; never in the repository or image.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Auto-configuration is a list in `.imports` files whose entries are filtered and guarded by conditions; user beans are processed first and make library beans back off.
- `--debug` and `/actuator/conditions` explain every decision; `/actuator/configprops` and `/actuator/env/<key>` explain every value and its origin.
- Relaxed binding accepts several spellings; kebab-case is canonical, environment variables drop dashes.
- The last property source wins: file, environment, system property, JSON, command line, test sources.
- A starter is an autoconfigure module plus an empty dependency module; test it with `ApplicationContextRunner`.
- Secrets belong in the platform, never in the repository.

A REST endpoint that appears to consist of one annotated method is, at run time, a pipeline of at least a dozen components: a socket acceptor, a worker thread, servlet filters, the `DispatcherServlet`, a handler mapping, interceptors, argument resolvers, the controller, a return-value handler, an HTTP message converter, and an exception resolver. Every observable symptom of a web defect (a 415 response, a request that hangs, a missing CORS header, a lazy-loading exception during JSON output) belongs to exactly one stage of this pipeline. This chapter follows one request through the stages in order, names the classes involved, and then applies the model to four kinds of defects.

### Concept and mechanism

#### From the socket to the DispatcherServlet

Spring Boot embeds Apache Tomcat (through `TomcatServletWebServerFactory`). The default connector is `Http11NioProtocol`. Its structure determines how many requests the service can process at once.

- An **acceptor** thread accepts new TCP connections and hands them to a **poller**, which watches the open sockets with a selector (NIO). Idle keep-alive connections cost a socket and a small buffer, not a thread.
- When a request is readable, the poller assigns a **worker thread** from the executor pool. The worker parses the HTTP request line and headers, runs the servlet filter chain and the `DispatcherServlet`, writes the response, and returns to the pool.
- The pool is bounded: `server.tomcat.threads.max` (default 200) and `server.tomcat.threads.min-spare` (default 10, threads kept ready).
- `server.tomcat.max-connections` (default 8192) limits connections that Tomcat accepts and watches. When that limit is reached the operating system queues further connections up to `server.tomcat.accept-count` (default 100); beyond it the connection attempt is refused.

The central fact is that with a blocking controller **one worker thread is occupied for the full duration of a** **request**, including time spent waiting for a database, a downstream service or a lock. Throughput is therefore bounded by `threads.max / mean request duration`.

blocks.text:
#### DispatcherServlet.doDispatch

Tomcat calls the servlet `service()` method, which `FrameworkServlet` routes to `processRequest()` and then to `DispatcherServlet.doService()` and `doDispatch()`. This method is the front controller of Spring MVC. Its steps, in order:

1. `getHandler()` iterates over the `HandlerMapping` beans in order (`RequestMappingHandlerMapping` for `@RequestMapping` methods, then `RouterFunctionMapping`, `BeanNameUrlHandlerMapping`, the static resource mapping) and returns a `HandlerExecutionChain`: the handler (a `HandlerMethod`) plus the applicable `HandlerInterceptor` list. When none matches, the result is a 404, or `NoHandlerFoundException` when configured.
2. `getHandlerAdapter()` selects the adapter that can invoke the handler (`RequestMappingHandlerAdapter` for `HandlerMethod`).
3. `HandlerInterceptor.preHandle()` is called in registration order. A `false` return stops the chain and triggers `afterCompletion` for the interceptors that already ran.
4. `RequestMappingHandlerAdapter.handle()` creates an `InvocableHandlerMethod`. Each parameter is filled by a `HandlerMethodArgumentResolver`: `@PathVariable`, `@RequestParam`, `@RequestHeader`, `@ModelAttribute` (form binding with validation), and `@RequestBody` (`RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor`, which reads the body through an `HttpMessageConverter` and applies `@Valid`).
5. The controller method runs.
6. A `HandlerMethodReturnValueHandler` processes the result. For `@ResponseBody` and `ResponseEntity` it selects an `HttpMessageConverter` by content negotiation and writes the body; for a view name it prepares a `ModelAndView`.
7. `postHandle()` is called in **reverse** order, then the result is rendered.
8. If any step threw an exception, `processHandlerException()` asks the `HandlerExceptionResolver` composite: `ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver` (methods annotated `@ExceptionHandler`, local to the controller or global through `@ControllerAdvice`), `ResponseStatusExceptionResolver` (`@ResponseStatus`, `ResponseStatusException`), and `DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver` (standard Spring exceptions mapped to 4xx and 5xx).
9. `afterCompletion()` is called in reverse order for every interceptor whose `preHandle` returned true, in all cases, including exceptions.

An exception that no resolver handles is rethrown to the container, which forwards to `/error`, served by `BasicErrorController`.

blocks.text: #### Filters versus interceptors

rows: Servlet specification; managed by the container
Before the DispatcherServlet; also sees static resources, /error and requests with no handler
Inside the DispatcherServlet, after the handler is chosen
Yes (HttpServletRequestWrapper), so it can replace the body or headers
No; it can only read and set attributes and headers
Yes (the handler argument is a HandlerMethod)
Must handle its own; @ExceptionHandler does not see them
Exceptions reach exception resolvers (preHandle) and afterCompletion
Security (Spring Security is a filter chain), request ID and MDC, compression, CORS
Per-handler timing, audit, locale, authorisation checks that need handler annotations
blocks.caption: Servlet filter versus Spring MVC interceptor.

blocks.text: A filter registered as a Spring bean is added to the servlet chain automatically (by `ServletContextInitializerBeans`); its order is controlled with `@Order` or `FilterRegistrationBean.setOrder`. The registered filters execute in that order before the `DispatcherServlet`; Spring Security's `DelegatingFilterProxy` participates in the same chain.

blocks.text:
#### Message conversion and content negotiation

The step that selects the representation is content negotiation. For a `@RequestBody` parameter, the converter is chosen by the request `Content-Type` against `consumes`; for the response, by the request `Accept` header, the `produces` condition of the mapping, and the converters registered. Boot registers, among others, `ByteArrayHttpMessageConverter`, `StringHttpMessageConverter` (UTF-8), `ResourceHttpMessageConverter`, and `MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter` when Jackson is on the classpath. The order matters: a method returning `String` is written by the string converter as `text/plain`, not as a JSON string.

rows: Malformed JSON, wrong type for a field, missing body when required
The Content-Type of the request is not consumed by any converter or by the `consumes` condition (for example form data posted to a JSON-only endpoint)
The Accept header lists only types the endpoint cannot produce (Accept: application/xml with Jackson only)
The path matches, the HTTP method does not

blocks.text:
`produces` *select the writing converter (406 when absent).*

Jackson's behaviour in Boot differs from a bare `ObjectMapper`: Boot builds the mapper with `Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilder` and disables `FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES` and `WRITE_DATES_AS_TIMESTAMPS`, registers the `jackson-datatype-jsr310` module so `java.time` types serialise as ISO-8601 strings, and honours the `spring.jackson.*` properties. Declaring a custom `ObjectMapper` bean makes the auto-configured one back off, and the application then loses these defaults; customise with a `Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer` bean instead.

#### Asynchronous request processing

A servlet container can release the worker thread while a result is pending: `request.startAsync()` detaches the request and the thread returns to the pool; when the result is ready, the container performs an **async dispatch** that passes through the `DispatcherServlet` again and writes the response. Spring MVC exposes this through controller return types:

- `Callable<T>`: Spring runs the callable on a `TaskExecutor` (in Boot, `applicationTaskExecutor`).
- `DeferredResult<T>` and `CompletableFuture<T>`: the application completes the result from any thread (a message listener, a client callback).
- `StreamingResponseBody` and `SseEmitter`: streaming output and server-sent events.

`spring.mvc.async.request-timeout` bounds the wait; an expired request yields a 503 via `AsyncRequestTimeoutException`. Asynchronous MVC does not make the downstream call non-blocking: a `Callable` that blocks on a database still occupies a thread, on the task executor instead of a Tomcat worker. The gain is real only when the work is fed by an event rather than computed by a blocked thread.

#### Virtual threads in Spring Boot 3.2 and later

Since Spring Boot 3.2 on Java 21, setting `spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true` configures Tomcat (and Jetty) to run each request on a **virtual thread** and switches the `applicationTaskExecutor` and scheduler to virtual-thread implementations. The blocking style of the controller code is unchanged; a blocked virtual thread unmounts from its carrier thread, so the limit of 200 workers no longer caps the number of concurrent requests that are waiting. Consequences that must be understood:

- The bottleneck moves downstream. A database pool of 10 connections still allows only 10 concurrent queries; thousands of waiting requests simply queue on the pool (and need a timeout, see the clients chapter).
- On JDK 21, blocking inside a `synchronized` block **pins** the virtual thread to its carrier, which reintroduces thread starvation; JDK 24 (JEP 491) removed the pinning for `synchronized`. Native calls and some file operations still pin.
- Code that relies on thread-pool bounds for load limiting (for example one pool per downstream) must introduce explicit limits such as semaphores or bulkheads (see the chapter on resilience).
- `ThreadLocal` values are per virtual thread and are not shared across requests; avoid caching large objects in thread locals.

A plain-JDK measurement that mirrors the effect is presented in the hands-on section.

#### Other mechanisms in brief

**File upload.** `MultipartFile` parameters are filled by `StandardServletMultipartResolver`. Limits are `spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size` (default 1MB) and `max-request-size` (default 10MB); exceeding either gives a 413-type failure (`MaxUploadSizeExceededException`, usually surfaced as 413 by Boot's error handling). For large files, stream with `file.getInputStream()` to the destination and never call `getBytes()`.

**CORS.** Cross-origin requests that are not "simple" are preceded by a preflight `OPTIONS` request with `Origin`, `Access-Control-Request-Method` and `Access-Control-Request-Headers`. Spring MVC answers it in the handler mapping (via `CorsFilter` or the `CorsProcessor` of `AbstractHandlerMapping`) according to `@CrossOrigin` or `addCorsMappings`, **without invoking the controller**. When Spring Security is present the preflight must also pass the security filter chain, which requires `http.cors(Customizer.withDefaults())` so that the CORS configuration is applied before authentication.

**HTTP caching.** A `ResponseEntity` with an `eTag(...)` or `lastModified(...)` header makes the framework answer a matching conditional `GET` (`If-None-Match`) with `304 Not Modified` and no body. `ShallowEtagHeaderFilter` computes the ETag from the generated body for any endpoint; it saves bandwidth, not server computation, because the body is still produced. `Cache-Control` is set with `CacheControl.maxAge(...)`.

**Pagination and sorting.** Spring Data's `PageableHandlerMethodArgumentResolver` converts `?page=0&size=20&sort=title,asc` into a `Pageable`. The default maximum page size is 2000 (`spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size`); public APIs should lower it. Sort property names are passed to the data layer, so they must be restricted to a whitelist of allowed properties. Return DTOs, not entities. **API versioning.** In Spring Framework 6.2 and Boot 3.x there is no first-class versioning mechanism; the practical strategies are a path prefix (`/api/v1/books`), a custom header (`X-API-Version`), and media-type versioning with the `produces` condition (`application/vnd.library.v2+json`). First-class version support (a `version` attribute on mappings and `spring.mvc.apiversion.*` properties) arrived with Spring Framework 7 and Boot 4. Whatever the strategy, a change that removes or renames a field requires a new version; adding optional fields does not.

**Error format.** `ProblemDetail` implements RFC 9457 (which obsoletes RFC 7807) with the members `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`, `instance` and extension members, served as `application/problem+json`. Extending `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler` converts all standard MVC exceptions to this format. If the application declares no such advice, `spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true` enables Boot's built-in equivalent.

### Worked example

The example is the REST API of a library: a paged book list with sorting, a single book with an ETag, creation with validation, a uniform error format, a request-ID filter, a timing interceptor and a CORS policy. The code is Spring Boot 3.x with `spring-boot-starter-web`, `spring-boot-starter-validation` and Spring Data Commons (for `Pageable`).

### Hands-on

Two plain-JDK programs reproduce the mechanisms of this chapter with real output. The first models the servlet filter chain and the `doDispatch` sequence: handler lookup, interceptor `preHandle`, `postHandle` and `afterCompletion` ordering, exception resolution, and short-circuiting by an interceptor.

blocks.title: MiniDispatcher.java

blocks.code:
$ java MiniDispatcher.java
GET /books
  CharacterEncodingFilter before
  SecurityFilter before
    A.preHandle -> true
    B.preHandle -> true
    B.postHandle
    A.postHandle
    B.afterCompletion ex=null
    A.afterCompletion ex=null
  SecurityFilter after  (status 200)
  CharacterEncodingFilter after  (status 200)
  => Response[status=200, body=[book1, book2]]
GET /boom
  CharacterEncodingFilter before
  SecurityFilter before
    A.preHandle -> true
    B.preHandle -> true
    B.afterCompletion ex=page must be >= 0
    A.afterCompletion ex=page must be >= 0
  SecurityFilter after  (status 400)
  CharacterEncodingFilter after  (status 400)
  => Response[status=400, body=page must be >= 0]
GET /missing
  CharacterEncodingFilter before
  SecurityFilter before
  SecurityFilter after  (status 404)
  CharacterEncodingFilter after  (status 404)
  => Response[status=404, body=no handler]
GET /books with interceptor B rejecting
  CharacterEncodingFilter before
  SecurityFilter before
    A.preHandle -> true
    B.preHandle -> false
    A.afterCompletion ex=null
  SecurityFilter after  (status 403)
  CharacterEncodingFilter after  (status 403)
  => Response[status=403, body=blocked]
blocks.title: Real run on the build machine (JDK 21)

blocks.text:
What to notice: for `/boom` the `postHandle` callbacks are skipped but both `afterCompletion` callbacks run and receive the exception; the filters see the final status 400 on the way out, which proves that exception resolution happens inside the dispatcher, before the filters unwind. For `/missing` no interceptor runs at all, because no handler was found, while both filters still run. When interceptor B rejects the request, only interceptor A (the one that already ran) receives `afterCompletion`.

The second program measures thread-per-request starvation. A pool of platform threads stands in for the Tomcat worker pool (scaled down from 200 to 10 and 50 threads) and each of 100 requests blocks for 200 ms, as a call to a slow downstream service would. The third line uses one virtual thread per request, which is what `spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true` configures.

blocks.title: PoolStarvation.java

blocks.code:
$ java PoolStarvation.java
100 requests, each blocks 200 ms
platform pool, 10 threads          total= 2015 ms  mean latency=1097 ms  worst=2002 ms
platform pool, 50 threads          total=  406 ms  mean latency= 298 ms  worst= 400 ms
virtual thread per request         total=  213 ms  mean latency= 203 ms  worst= 209 ms
blocks.title: Measured on the build machine (2 CPUs, JDK 21); timings vary slightly between runs

blocks.text:
The first row shows the mechanism of starvation: 100 requests of 200 ms through 10 workers need ten waves of 200 ms, so the last request waits about 2 seconds although each request needs only 200 ms of actual work; the mean latency of 1.1 seconds is queueing delay. The relation is Little's law: sustained concurrency equals arrival rate multiplied by latency. A service receiving 100 requests per second whose downstream call takes 5 seconds needs 500 concurrent workers, and a pool of 200 cannot supply them. The virtual-thread row removes the pool as the limit; the remaining limit would be the downstream capacity.
